justification_text:
At the time of this forecast, the asset appeared to be trading near the $91–92 range, which anchored my short-term point estimate. For the one-day horizon, I leaned on mean-reversion tendencies and the assumption that no major catalysts were imminent, placing the estimate at $91.8 with a relatively tight confidence interval. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher to $92.1, reflecting a mild upward drift assumption consistent with modest positive momentum, while the one-month estimate of $93.0 incorporated a longer-run drift component that assumes gradual appreciation under stable macro conditions.

The confidence interval widths were deliberately scaled to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the $88.5–$95.1 range captures typical intraday-to-next-day volatility, essentially one to two standard deviations of daily price movement. By one week, the interval widens to $84.8–$99.4, accounting for the accumulation of daily shocks over several trading sessions. The one-month interval of $78–$108 is quite wide by design, reflecting the reality that over four weeks, macro shifts, earnings surprises, sector rotations, or liquidity events can move prices substantially in either direction. Historical volatility was the primary quantitative input driving these widths.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden changes in central bank policy signals, unexpected geopolitical developments, or a sharp dislocation in correlated markets such as credit spreads or currency pairs. On the upside, a short squeeze, positive earnings revision, or sector-wide rotation into the relevant asset class could drive prices well above $99 or even $108 within the stated windows. On the downside, a risk-off episode triggered by inflation data surprises, banking stress, or a global growth scare could break below $88 or $78 more quickly than the intervals suggest.

It is also worth acknowledging model limitations. My intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, but real markets exhibit fat tails, meaning truly extreme moves happen more frequently than a normal distribution would predict. A black swan event — a flash crash, a liquidity freeze, or an unexpected geopolitical shock — could render all three intervals simultaneously too narrow. Conversely, if the asset enters a very low-volatility regime, actual realized prices could stay well within even the tightest interval throughout the entire month.
